rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether a multimodal model (combining RNA + image) provides meaningful benefit over unimodal baselines, and what a reasonable 'simple multimodal' performance level looks like. Config_018 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, weighted fusion) is the simplest reasonable multimodal configuration: it uses the most straightforward RNA encoder (PCA, no learned parameters), a standard image backbone (ResNet-50), single-profile (no aggregation needed), and weighted fusion. This establishes a central anchor in the design space from which many one-parameter comparisons can be drawn in subsequent experiments: removing RNA (config_004) isolates the image-only baseline, removing image (config_046) isolates the RNA-only baseline, swapping the RNA encoder (config_019 scvi, config_036 scgpt) tests whether learned representations add value over linear dimensionality reduction, swapping the image encoder (config_021 ViT-L) tests backbone quality, and changing fusion (config_009 concat) tests fusion strategy. Starting here maximizes the number of informative follow-up comparisons per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_018: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion → 52.3% acc). With a single data point, the most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA modality actually contributes to performance or whether the image alone accounts for most of the signal. Question: config_004 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean ablation of config_018 with only the RNA modality removed, isolating the effect of multimodality. Why this is the best next experiment: Without an image-only baseline, we cannot interpret any future multimodal result—improvements could come from better image features, RNA contribution, or fusion interactions. Establishing this reference point first ensures that all subsequent experiments (varying RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion) are interpreted against a meaningful unimodal floor. It is a single-variable change, maximally informative, and essential before investing budget in more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, singleprofile, weighted) achieves 0.523 acc while config_004 (image_only, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208 acc, a ~31 pp gap. However, we have no RNA-only data point, so we cannot decompose how much of the multimodal performance comes from the RNA modality versus the image modality or their interaction. Question: config_046 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no image, no aggregation, no fusion) isolates the RNA contribution using the same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_018, with no other confounds. Why best next experiment: With only two completed runs, the single most important uncertainty is the per-modality contribution. Knowing RNA-only accuracy lets us determine whether the multimodal gain is driven primarily by RNA (suggesting we should invest in better RNA encoders like scgpt/scvi) or by the image+RNA interaction (suggesting we should focus on fusion and image encoder upgrades). This single clean comparison maximally reduces uncertainty before committing further budget to more complex multiprofile or aggregation variants.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000) alone achieves 0.485 acc while image (resnet50) alone is only 0.208, and the multimodal model (config_018) reaches 0.523—only a ~4% gain over RNA alone. This indicates RNA is the dominant signal and the current linear PCA representation may be a bottleneck. Uncertainty: We have only tested a linear RNA encoder (pca_n2000); it is unknown whether a learned encoder (scgpt) captures non-linear biological structure that would substantially improve both the RNA baseline and the multimodal model. This experiment (config_007: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, weighted fusion) changes exactly one variable relative to config_018—the RNA encoder—so the result cleanly isolates the effect of RNA representation quality. If scgpt yields a meaningful accuracy/F1 gain over config_018, it tells us the RNA representation is the primary lever for improvement and justifies further investment in learned encoders; if not, PCA is near-sufficient and we should pivot to image encoder quality or fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, testing the dominant modality's representation first is the highest-information single experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted) achieved 0.523 acc, only modestly above RNA-only pca_n2000 (0.485), while image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208). This suggests the image branch may be a bottleneck in the multimodal model. Question: Does replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l (a stronger image encoder) improve multimodal performance? config_008 is identical to config_018 except for the image encoder, making it a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates the image representation effect. Why this is the best next step: Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image encoder is the limiting factor is the highest-value uncertainty. If imagenet_vit_l substantially lifts multimodal accuracy, it justifies investing further in image-heavy configurations; if not, we can focus budget on RNA encoder and profile/aggregation choices instead. This avoids the risk of prematurely exploring multiprofile or fusion variants on top of a weak image backbone.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) is the current best at 0.532 acc / 0.516 F1, slightly ahead of config_018 (same but resnet50, 0.523). RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.485 alone vs 0.208 for image), and pca_n2000 substantially outperforms scgpt (0.523 vs 0.421). The only fusion strategy tested so far is 'weighted'; we have no evidence about whether 'concat' could be superior. Question: config_021 is identical to config_008 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, giving a clean single-variable comparison to isolate the effect of fusion strategy with the best-known encoder pair. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the strongest result with a minimal change, reducing uncertainty about whether a different fusion mechanism could push performance higher before we invest budget in more complex multiprofile/aggregation designs. If concat matches or beats weighted, it reshapes the design space; if it underperforms, it confirms weighted as the preferred fusion and lets us focus subsequent experiments on profile setting and aggregation.

Evidence: The best singleprofile configuration is config_021 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat, acc=0.5353), with PCA clearly superior to scgpt for RNA and ViT-L slightly better than ResNet50. However, the multiprofile axis is completely unexplored—zero completed experiments use it. This is the largest remaining source of uncertainty about whether additional profile information (with aggregation) can push performance beyond the current ~0.535 ceiling. Question: Does adding multiple profiles with transformer aggregation, while holding the best-known encoders (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (concat) constant, improve over the singleprofile baseline? Why this experiment: config_042 is the most direct logical extension of config_021, changing only the profile setting and adding transformer aggregation. If it outperforms config_021, we confirm multiprofile is beneficial and can then explore aggregation variants; if it underperforms, we learn that the added complexity does not help and can redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., scvi_n200). Testing transformer first is informative because it is the most expressive aggregation—if even this fails to help, simpler aggregations (avgpool) are unlikely to succeed.

The largest performance jump in the history is from config_021 (singleprofile, no aggregation, concat: 0.535) to config_042 (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat: 0.599), a ~6-point gain. However, this comparison conflates two changes: (1) switching to multiprofile and (2) introducing transformer aggregation. Config_016 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) changes only the aggregation from transformer to avgpool while holding all other settings identical to config_042. This directly tests whether the transformer's sequential modeling of profiles is the critical driver or whether any aggregation of multiple profiles (even simple averaging) captures most of the gain. If avgpool approaches transformer performance, the multiprofile representation itself is the key factor (and a cheaper model suffices); if it falls well short, transformer aggregation is essential. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about the aggregation design choice before committing further budget to the multiprofile+transformer family.

The current best configuration (config_016: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + vit_l + pca_n2000 is the dominant design, but the fusion choice at the avgpool level is untested: concat gave 0.629 (config_016) and 0.599 with transformer (config_042), while weighted gave 0.532 in singleprofile (config_008) and 0.599 is untested with avgpool. Config_041 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a single-variable change from the current best, isolating the fusion effect at the top aggregation level. If weighted outperforms concat here, we identify a new best; if not, we confirm concat is the optimal fusion and can redirect remaining budget toward RNA encoder exploration (e.g., scvi_n200). This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_041: multiprofile, pca_n2000, vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.6352) establishes a strong baseline. We have clear evidence that PCA outperforms scgpt (0.5232 vs 0.4214 in singleprofile), but scvi_n200 has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Config_049 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other settings at their best-known values (multiprofile, vit_l, avgpool, weighted). This single-variable test directly answers whether a learned variational RNA encoder can capture complementary signal beyond PCA's linear dimensionality reduction. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it opens a new promising axis; if it underperforms, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward other unexplored dimensions. This is more informative than completing the aggregation×fusion 2×2 (config_047), where the avgpool>transformer gap (0.6287 vs 0.5988) is already large and the marginal information gain would be small.
